notes.meaning: A husband who found something indecent or offensive in his wife was permitted to write her an official certificate of divorce before sending her away. This written document gave the woman legal proof that her marriage was dissolved so that she could not later be accused of adultery. Moses did not establish divorce as God's ideal here, but regulated an existing practice to protect wives from being cast out unfairly.

Once the woman left her former husband's home with her certificate of divorce, she was legally free to marry someone else. In the ancient world, an unmarried woman had few ways to survive without the protection and support of a family household. The law treated her second marriage as fully valid and recognized under the civil code.

The case continues by describing what happens if the second husband also turns against her and issues a divorce, or if he dies. In either situation, the woman is once again left without a husband and released from that second marriage bond. Her departure or widowhood sets up the legal restriction that follows in the next verse.

The law firmly forbids the first husband from ever taking his former wife back after she has been married to someone else. She is regarded as defiled in relation to him, and taking her back would treat the marriage bond lightly and bring spiritual guilt upon the entire land. This rule made divorce a weighty and final step, preventing men from treating marriage casually or passing women between households.

differ.view: Some hold that this passage shows the original marriage bond is never fully undone, so any remarriage while a former spouse is still living is unlawful.
Many teach that Scripture permits divorce and remarriage in cases of sexual unfaithfulness or abandonment, viewing Moses' law as a merciful regulation rather than an absolute ban on all remarriage.

notes.meaning: A newly married man was completely excused from military service and public duties for one full year. This break allowed the couple to build a peaceful household and gave the husband time to bring joy to his bride. Protecting the foundation of a new family was considered more important than adding another soldier to the army.

Lenders were forbidden from taking a household handmill or even its upper grinding stone as security for a loan. Families relied on these stones every morning to grind flour for their daily bread. Taking the tool a family needed to feed themselves was treated as taking their very life away.

Anyone caught kidnapping a fellow Israelite to force them into slavery or sell them was condemned to death. Stealing a person destroyed their freedom and was treated with the same seriousness as taking a human life. Enforcing this penalty purged such cruelty from the nation and protected the vulnerable from exploitation.

In all outbreaks of serious and infectious skin diseases, the people were commanded to follow every instruction given by the Levitical priests. God had provided clear quarantine and diagnosis guidelines in the law of Moses to keep disease from spreading through the community. Obeying these rules preserved public health and guarded the ceremonial purity of the camp.

The people were reminded of what happened to Miriam when God struck her with a skin disease during their wilderness journey. Even though she was Moses' sister and a respected prophetess, she was required to remain outside the camp for seven full days. This showed that God's health laws applied equally to all people, without special favors for the wealthy or powerful.

When making a loan to a neighbor, the lender was not permitted to walk into the borrower's house to collect an item as security. Entering another person's home uninvited would show greed and expose the borrower's poverty to humiliation. God's law defended the privacy and personal honor of even the poorest debtor.

The lender had to wait in the street outside while the borrower brought out the item offered as collateral. This allowed the borrower to offer what he could best spare rather than having his essential goods taken by force. God required lenders to conduct business with patience, courtesy, and respect.

If the borrower was poor and gave his outer cloak as collateral, the lender was forbidden from keeping it overnight. For an impoverished person, an outer garment served as both daily clothing and a sleeping blanket. Holding on to it while the debtor froze showed a callous spirit that the law would not tolerate.

The lender was required to return the pledged cloak by sunset so the poor man could sleep in comfort. The debtor would bless the merciful lender in prayer, and the Lord would credit this kindness as true righteousness. God counts practical compassion toward the poor as genuine obedience to His covenant.

Employers were forbidden from taking advantage of hired workers who were poor and in need, whether they were fellow Israelites or resident foreigners. Day laborers had no land or savings, which made them especially easy targets for unfair treatment. God demanded that foreign workers receive the very same justice and honesty as native citizens.

Wages were to be paid at the end of every workday before the sun went down. Because poor laborers lived hand-to-mouth, their families depended on each day's earnings to buy their evening meal. Withholding a worker's wages was a sin that would move God to act if the mistreated laborer cried out to Him.

Judges and civil rulers were forbidden from putting parents to death for crimes committed by their children, or children for crimes committed by their parents. Every person was to answer solely for their own guilt in a court of law. This rule protected innocent family members from being wiped out because of a relative's wrongdoing.

The community was commanded never to rob foreigners or fatherless children of justice, nor to take a widow's cloak as debt collateral. These three groups had no family protectors in society and were easily cheated in legal disputes. God placed strict safeguards around them to ensure they received fair treatment in every situation.

Moses urged the people to remember that they had once been mistreated slaves in Egypt until the Lord redeemed them, which means He paid the cost to set them free. Remembering their own rescue from oppression was meant to stir up genuine mercy toward people in distress. Those who have experienced God's grace are called to treat others with the same kindness.

Farmers harvesting grain who forgot a bundle in the field were not allowed to go back and retrieve it. That leftover sheaf belonged to the resident foreigners, orphans, and widows so they could gather food for their tables. This practice provided for the poor with dignity and promised God's blessing on the farmer's remaining crop.

When farmers beat their olive trees to knock down the fruit, they were not to strip the branches a second time. Any olives left behind were set apart for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Leaving fruit on the trees ensured that needy neighbors could feed themselves through their own honest labor.

The same rule applied to the grape harvest: owners were forbidden from picking their vines clean after the first harvest run. The remaining clusters were left for the poor and fatherless to glean. God designed this system so that landowners shared the land's bounty without embarrassing those who needed help.

The chapter concludes with a final reminder of Israel's long years of slavery in the land of Egypt. Because the Lord had shown them generous mercy in their time of helplessness, He commanded them to show that same generosity to the weak. Remembering where they came from was intended to keep their hearts humble and giving.
